subject: Bio
title: Cells, molecules & enzymes
sub: Living things and classification, cells, diffusion and osmosis, food tests, enzymes
strategyIntro: Cambridge Core Biology is assessed on Paper 1 (40 multiple-choice questions, 45 min), Paper 3 (structured theory questions, 1h 15, 80 marks) and Paper 6 (questions on experiments). Your school test may be shorter, but it will be marked the same way.

strategy.title: Multiple choice
points: About a minute per question. If one is taking longer, mark it and move on.
Cross out options you know are wrong first. Two often look similar: read every word.
Never leave one blank. A wrong answer loses nothing.

strategy.title: Structured questions
points: Marks go to keywords. Write the textbook term: “oviduct”, not “tube”.
The marks in brackets tell you how many separate points to make.
Label diagrams with a ruler line that touches the exact part.

strategy.title: Questions on experiments
points: Results tables: units go in the column headings, not next to each number.
Graphs: label both axes with units, choose an even scale, plot with small crosses.
Know the control variables and one safety precaution for each experiment.

strategy.title: Easy marks people lose
points: Writing “growth is getting bigger”. Growth is a permanent increase in size and dry mass.
Giving magnification a unit. It is just “×400”. Convert to the same units first (1 mm = 1000 µm).
Saying enzymes are “killed”. They are proteins, not alive: they are denatured.
Forgetting “partially permeable membrane” in the definition of osmosis.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
quizIntro: Answer in Paper 1 style: about a minute each, eliminating wrong options first. Read the explanation after every answer, even when you get it right.
flashIntro: These are close to Cambridge’s own wording. Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.front: The seven characteristics of living organisms
flashcards.back: Movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition (MRS GREN).
The chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism.
The ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment.
A permanent increase in size and dry mass.
Removal of the waste products of metabolism, toxic materials and substances in excess of requirements.
A group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.
Naming a species with two names: the genus first (capital letter), then the species, e.g. Homo sapiens.
A key that identifies organisms by a series of steps, each giving a choice between two statements.
Mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
Fur or hair, external ears (pinnae), mammary glands that make milk; most give birth to live young.
Controls what enters and leaves the cell.
Contains the genetic material (DNA in chromosomes) that controls the cell’s activities.
Where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy.
Where proteins are made (protein synthesis).
Found in plant cells, made of cellulose. Strengthens the cell and stops it bursting.
Contains chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis. Plant cells only.
Large space filled with cell sap. Keeps a plant cell firm (turgid).
Cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, a circular DNA loop and plasmids. No nucleus.
Ciliated cells move mucus; root hair cells absorb water and ions; palisade cells photosynthesise; neurones carry impulses; red blood cells carry oxygen.
Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Use the same units for both; 1 mm = 1000 µm.
The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, as a result of their random movement.
None from the cell: it is passive. The particles’ own kinetic energy (random movement) drives it.
Larger surface area, higher temperature, steeper concentration gradient, shorter distance.
The net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
A membrane that lets small molecules such as water through but not larger ones such as sucrose.
Water enters by osmosis, the vacuole swells and the cell becomes turgid. The cell wall stops it bursting.

flashcards.front: Plant cell in a concentrated solution
flashcards.back: Water leaves by osmosis; the cell becomes flaccid and the membrane may pull away from the wall (plasmolysis).
Water enters by osmosis; the cell swells and may burst because it has no cell wall.
Movement of particles through a cell membrane from lower to higher concentration (against the gradient), using energy from respiration.
Root hair cells taking in mineral ions (e.g. nitrate) from the soil, where they are at a lower concentration.
Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (some also contain sulfur).
Made from many glucose molecules joined together.
Made from amino acids.
Made from fatty acids and glycerol.
Tests for starch: orange-brown → blue-black.
Tests for reducing sugars (e.g. glucose): heat in a hot water bath; blue → green, yellow, orange or brick red.
Tests for protein: blue → purple (lilac).
Tests for fats and oils: shake with ethanol, then add water; a cloudy white emulsion forms.
Tests for vitamin C: blue DCPIP loses its colour.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction.
A protein that functions as a biological catalyst.
They speed up the reactions in cells enough to keep the organism alive at body temperature.
The region on an enzyme where the substrate binds.
The molecule an enzyme acts on, e.g. starch for amylase.
The active site has a shape complementary to the substrate, so each enzyme only works on one substrate.
The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest: about 37 °C for human enzymes.
Enzymes work slowly: molecules have less kinetic energy, so there are fewer collisions. The enzyme is not damaged.
High temperature or the wrong pH changes the shape of the active site, so the substrate no longer fits. This is permanent.
Each enzyme works best at one pH, e.g. the protease in the stomach works best in acid (about pH 2).

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of all living organisms?
quiz.why: Only plants (and some other organisms) photosynthesise. The characteristic all organisms share is nutrition.

quiz.q: The lion is Panthera leo. What does “Panthera” tell you?
quiz.why: In the binomial system the first name is the genus and the second is the species.

quiz.q: An animal has dry, scaly skin and lays eggs with rubbery shells on land. Which group is it in?
quiz.why: Reptiles have dry scales and lay shelled eggs on land. Amphibians have moist skin and lay eggs in water; birds have feathers.

quiz.q: Which is the best definition of growth?
options: An increase in the number of cells
A permanent increase in size and dry mass
quiz.why: Growth must be permanent and is measured as dry mass, so water taken in does not count.

quiz.q: Removing carbon dioxide from the body is an example of:
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide is a waste product of metabolism (respiration). Egestion is getting rid of undigested food, which was never made by cells.

quiz.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
quiz.why: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. Animal cells have the other three.

quiz.q: Which structure do bacterial cells NOT have?
quiz.why: Bacteria have no nucleus: their DNA is a circular loop free in the cytoplasm, plus small rings called plasmids.

quiz.q: A drawing of a cell is 15 mm long. The magnification is ×300. What is the actual length of the cell?
quiz.why: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 15 ÷ 300 = 0.05 mm (50 µm).

quiz.q: What is the function of ciliated cells lining the trachea?
options: Moving mucus up and away from the lungs
quiz.why: Cilia beat to sweep mucus, with trapped dust and pathogens, up to the throat.

quiz.q: Which order of organisation is correct, from smallest to largest?
quiz.why: Similar cells form a tissue, tissues form an organ, organs work together in an organ system.

quiz.q: Where does aerobic respiration happen in a cell?
quiz.why: Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration. Ribosomes make proteins; chloroplasts photosynthesise.

quiz.q: How does oxygen move from the alveoli into the blood?
quiz.why: Oxygen is at a higher concentration in the alveoli than in the blood, so it diffuses across.

quiz.q: A potato cylinder is left in concentrated sugar solution for an hour. What happens?
options: Its mass increases as water enters
Its mass decreases as water leaves by osmosis
Its mass increases as sugar enters
quiz.why: The solution is more concentrated than the potato cells, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis.

quiz.q: Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?
quiz.why: More surface area means more particles can cross at once. The other three all slow diffusion down.

quiz.q: Red blood cells burst in pure water but plant cells do not. Why?
options: Plant cells have a cell wall
Red blood cells have no nucleus
quiz.why: Both cells take in water by osmosis, but the strong cellulose cell wall stops a plant cell bursting.

quiz.q: Which process needs energy from respiration?
quiz.why: Active transport moves particles against a concentration gradient, so it needs energy. Diffusion and osmosis are passive.

quiz.q: Which reagent is used to test for protein?
quiz.why: Biuret turns from blue to purple with protein. Iodine is for starch, Benedict’s for reducing sugar, ethanol for fats.

quiz.q: A food sample turns blue-black when iodine solution is added. It contains:
quiz.why: Iodine goes from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present.

quiz.q: Proteins are made from:
quiz.why: Amino acids join in long chains to make proteins. Glucose builds starch; fatty acids and glycerol build fats.

quiz.q: Which food test needs heating?
quiz.why: Benedict’s solution must be heated in a hot water bath before the colour change appears.

quiz.q: Which element is found in proteins but not in carbohydrates?
quiz.why: Carbohydrates contain only C, H and O. Proteins also contain nitrogen.

quiz.q: What is an enzyme?
options: A carbohydrate that speeds up reactions
A protein that is a biological catalyst
A hormone carried in the blood
quiz.why: All enzymes are proteins, and they catalyse reactions without being used up.

quiz.q: The rate of an enzyme reaction rises up to 40 °C, then falls quickly. Why does it fall?
options: The enzyme has too much energy
The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
quiz.why: Above the optimum the enzyme is denatured: its active site loses its shape.

quiz.q: At 5 °C an enzyme reaction is very slow. Why?
options: Molecules move slowly, so there are fewer collisions
quiz.why: Cold slows molecules down. The enzyme is not denatured: warm it up and it works again.

quiz.q: Amylase breaks down starch but not protein. Why?
options: Only starch fits the shape of amylase’s active site
Protein is not a substrate for any enzyme
quiz.why: Enzymes are specific: the active site is complementary to one substrate only.

quiz.q: What does amylase break starch down into?
quiz.why: Amylase digests starch to simple sugars. Proteases make amino acids; lipases make fatty acids and glycerol.

examIntro: Paper 3 style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme and give yourself one mark per point you made clearly. One point per mark is the rule.

exam.q: State two features that all mammals have but fish do not.
points: Fur / hair
Mammary glands / feed young on milk
External ears (pinnae)
Lungs (fish have gills)

exam.q: A student says a car is alive because it moves, uses fuel and gives out waste gases. Explain why a car is not a living organism.
points: It does not grow (no permanent increase in dry mass)
It cannot reproduce
It is not sensitive / cannot detect and respond to stimuli by itself
It is not made of cells
Burning fuel is combustion, not respiration in cells
exam.note: Any 3. Use the characteristics of living things by name.

exam.q: Define the term species and explain how the binomial system is used to name humans, Homo sapiens.
points: Species: a group of organisms that can reproduce
to produce fertile offspring
Each species has two names
Homo is the genus
sapiens is the species

exam.q: State the function of (a) the nucleus and (b) the cell membrane.
points: (a) Contains genetic material / controls the activities of the cell
(b) Controls what enters and leaves the cell

exam.q: A drawing of a cell is 60 mm long. The real cell is 0.12 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working.
points: magnification = image size ÷ actual size
= ×500 (no units)

exam.q: Name three structures found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell, and state the function of each.
points: Cell wall
Strengthens the cell / keeps its shape / stops it bursting
Chloroplast
Absorbs light for photosynthesis
Large permanent vacuole
Contains cell sap / keeps the cell turgid for support
exam.note: One mark for each structure, one for its matching function.

Through a partially permeable membrane

exam.q: Describe and explain what happens to a plant cell placed in pure water.
points: Water moves into the cell
By osmosis
Through the partially permeable membrane
Because the cell sap is more concentrated than the water
The vacuole swells and the cell becomes turgid
The cell wall stops the cell bursting

exam.q: A student put one potato cylinder in distilled water and one in concentrated sugar solution for an hour. The first gained mass and the second lost mass. Explain these results and state two variables the student should keep the same.
points: In water: water entered the cells by osmosis, as the cell contents were more concentrated
In sugar solution: water left the cells by osmosis, into the more concentrated solution
Through partially permeable membranes
Control: starting size / length / mass of the cylinders
Control: temperature
Control: time left in the solution / volume of solution / same potato
exam.note: Up to 3 for the explanation, 2 for the variables.

exam.q: Name the smaller molecules that make up (a) starch and (b) fats.
points: (a) Glucose
(b) Fatty acids and glycerol

exam.q: Describe how to test a food for reducing sugar. Include the positive result.
points: Add Benedict’s solution to the food (in solution)
Heat in a hot water bath
Colour changes from blue to (green, yellow, orange or) brick red

exam.q: Describe how you would test a liquid food to find out whether it contains starch and protein. Give the result for each if the substance is present.
points: Add iodine solution
Turns blue-black if starch is present (stays orange-brown if not)
Add biuret reagent (or sodium hydroxide then copper sulfate solution)
Turns purple / lilac if protein is present
Stays blue if no protein
A protein
That is a biological catalyst / speeds up a reaction without being changed

exam.q: Explain why an enzyme only works on one type of substrate.
points: The enzyme has an active site
with a specific shape
that is complementary to / fits only its substrate (lock and key)
Other molecules do not fit the active site

exam.q: Describe and explain how temperature affects the rate of a reaction controlled by an enzyme.
points: As temperature increases the rate increases, up to the optimum
Molecules have more kinetic energy, so more collisions between enzyme and substrate
Optimum (for human enzymes) is about 37 °C
Above the optimum the rate falls quickly
The enzyme is denatured
The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
